knownOutputs.headline: Oregon by 28 in the Coliseum and Riley Gone by Halloween: The Firing Is the Easy Part
knownOutputs.dek: A listener wants Oregon to beat USC by four touchdowns on September 26 and Lincoln Riley fired before Halloween. The number I had checked came back at 6.5. That gap, not the firing, is why this one rates a 9.75.
knownOutputs.bodyMarkdown:
Every August I close the show by rating your bold predictions instead of mine, and the first one out of the box this year arrived from Diamond, Ohio, with two clauses stapled together. Dan Lanning and Oregon walk into the Coliseum on September 26 and beat USC by 28 or more. Lincoln Riley is fired before Halloween.

I rated it a 9.75, and those two clauses are nowhere close to equally hard. The firing is not a long shot. The margin is. If USC is bad enough to get drugged by four touchdowns at home, that's probably not the only game they're losing before Halloween, which means the second half of this prediction largely takes care of itself. The 28-plus number is the only part of it that can cost somebody the win.

[EMBED:00:00:58]

Oregon is No. 2 in the AP poll off a 13-2 season, and this is a program that has already proven it can go on the road in this league and take a game away from a good team in the first twenty minutes. USC is No. 14 off 9-4, at home, in a stadium where the Trojans have not been anybody's punching bag. I was curious enough about the number that I had Mike at FanDuel price it, and it came back around Oregon by 6.5. Twenty-eight is more than four times that.

[PULLQUOTE]

Understand what a 28-point road win actually requires, because it is not simply the favorite playing well. Oregon has to control the line of scrimmage on first and second down for four quarters so that USC lives in third-and-7 all afternoon. The Trojans have to waste possessions early, when their scripted plays are supposed to be their best ones. And somewhere in there Oregon needs a short field it did not earn with a drive, because scores of that size get built from possessions the trailing team never gets back. That happens in this sport a few Saturdays a year. It is not the middle outcome of a game the market believes is inside a touchdown.

The part of this prediction that is genuinely live has nothing to do with the margin. USC opens with San José State on August 29, Fresno State on September 4, Louisiana on September 12, and a trip to Rutgers on September 19. The reasonable expectation is that the Trojans are 4-0 and ranked when Oregon walks in, and 4-0 raises the floor of what the building expects.

Then look at what comes after Oregon. Washington comes to the Coliseum on October 3. USC goes to Penn State on October 10. After an open week, it goes to Wisconsin on October 24, a late-October Big Ten road game against a team that will try to make it a 20-carry, 60-minute physical argument. Every one of those three is a losable game for a team that just got beaten at home, and they stack in the ugliest possible order: a home loss, then Beaver Stadium, then a cold-weather trip nobody in Los Angeles enjoys explaining.

That path does not require a single blowout.

So name the realistic alternative, because it is the version of this that gets a fan base what it wants and gets the prediction nothing. USC loses to Oregon by 21 instead of 28. Every domino stands. Washington is still a live loss, Penn State is still a road loss waiting to happen, Wisconsin in late October is still Wisconsin in late October, and the argument about Riley's job is fully intact in the middle of the month. The prediction is dead anyway, because it specified a number that Saturday did not produce.

The second trap is the calendar, and it is stranger than the margin. Ohio State comes to the Coliseum on October 31. The game that looks most like a death blow on USC's schedule is the one game that cannot be the trigger, because the prediction requires Riley to be gone before Halloween. USC would have to fire its head coach during the week it is selling the biggest home date of its season and hand that Saturday to an interim staff. Everything here has to be executed inside the five weeks between September 26 and October 30.

Here is my concession, with dates on it. If Oregon wins by 30 on September 26, I will say on the air that night that the firing clause is close to a formality. And by the time USC finishes with Washington on October 3 and Penn State on October 10, we will know whether the firing conversation ever needed the blowout at all.

## What I'm Watching

September 26 in the Coliseum, Lanning against Riley, with the number saying 6.5 and the prediction demanding 28. October 3 and October 10, Washington at home and the trip to Penn State, which together decide whether the hot-seat talk becomes real without any help from Oregon. October 31, Ohio State walking into the Coliseum with either an interim coach on the USC sideline or the guy everybody assumed would be there in August.

So I'll plant it. The firing half is live enough that I would not talk anybody out of it, and my call is that the margin half breaks: Oregon wins that game by fewer than 28. That one gets graded the second the final score goes up on September 26, and the Riley half gets graded on the last day of October. If I have it backward, I will say so with my name on it.

That is why this stays a 9.75 and not something in the sevens. Not because Riley is safe. Because 28 is a very specific number, and specific numbers are how bold predictions die one touchdown short.

— JP

knownOutputs.dek: Dan from Diamond, Ohio, picked Oregon to win at the Coliseum by at least 28 points on September 26 and Lincoln Riley to be fired before Halloween. I rated the prediction a 9.75 because the 28, not the coaching change, is what makes the call so difficult.
knownOutputs.bodyMarkdown:
Every bold prediction has a headline people remember and a detail that decides whether the chalice ever leaves the building. Dan from Diamond, Ohio, gave me both: Oregon by 28 or more at the Coliseum on September 26, then Lincoln Riley fired before Halloween. I rated it a 9.75.

The firing is not the boldest part. The 28 is. Oregon being good enough to win that game is easy to understand. Oregon winning by four touchdowns is a different demand, and the exact margin is what turns a reasonable prediction about Riley's job into one of the hardest calls on the board.

[EMBED:00:00:53]

[PULLQUOTE]

## The margin is the bet

The early FanDuel number I checked on this game was Oregon minus 6.5. That is a meaningful favorite, and it makes sense. Oregon enters the season ranked No. 2 in both preseason polls after going 13-2 in 2025. USC went 9-4 and finished 7-2 in its first Big Ten season, but the Trojans open No. 14. This is a game with a clear favorite. It is not a game separated by four touchdowns before kickoff.

Dan's prediction asks Oregon to beat that number by at least 21.5 points. A 28-point win is not simply Oregon winning the game it is expected to win. It requires the Ducks to turn a six-point expectation into a result so large that the margin becomes the story before anybody reaches the coaching question.

That difference lives in the ordinary parts of a football game. Oregon has to turn field position into touchdowns instead of field goals. It has to prevent USC from answering after scores. It has to create enough long-yardage downs that the Trojans cannot keep the game inside one or two possessions. Oregon can be the better team and still win by 10. It can control the game and still fail this prediction by 11 points.

That is the weak link. Not Oregon. Not even the idea that USC could be in a difficult place by late September. The weak link is demanding that the difference between these teams show up as 28 points on one afternoon.

## USC can reach September 26 with a case intact

USC's September schedule before Oregon is San José State on August 29, Fresno State on September 4, Louisiana on September 12, and Rutgers on September 19. The Trojans can reach the Coliseum with a clean record and a No. 14 ranking still attached to them. They will not arrive looking like a four-touchdown underdog.

That matters because USC is not walking into this game as a program already stripped of every reasonable argument. The Trojans won nine games last season and went 7-2 in conference play. Their first four opponents do not force the kind of early September gauntlet that would make a collapse obvious before Oregon arrives. On September 25, the season can still look intact.

Then Oregon can win by 28 anyway. That is the tension inside the prediction. The result would be devastating, but the path to it is not visible in the preseason record. Oregon is favored by roughly 6.5, not 28, and USC's four-game runway gives Riley a chance to arrive at the matchup with a season that still presents a defense.

The realistic alternative is that Oregon wins by 21 to 27, USC absorbs the loss, and Riley reaches October. That result would say Oregon was clearly better without proving the Trojans had become a four-touchdown home mismatch. The alternative falls short of Dan's call because 27 and 28 are two different worlds here. One is a major loss. The other activates the exact margin that makes this prediction a 9.75.

## The schedule can decide Riley's future without Oregon's help

The Riley portion of the prediction has a much more direct path than the margin. After Oregon, USC hosts Washington on October 3, travels to Penn State on October 10, and visits Wisconsin on October 24. Those are three more chances to lose before Ohio State arrives at the Coliseum on October 31.

Washington gets the first opportunity. Penn State supplies the most demanding road test in the immediate stretch. Wisconsin creates another road result before the deadline. The games are close enough together that a bad Oregon loss does not have to stand alone. A 28-point defeat on September 26 could become the first piece of a four-week sequence that makes the decision unavoidable.

If USC is bad enough to get dragged by four touchdowns at home, that is probably not the only game it loses before Halloween. The margin supplies the alarm. The schedule supplies the additional evidence.

But the deadline makes the prediction harder again. Ohio State comes to the Coliseum on October 31. That is Halloween itself. Before Halloween means Riley has to be dismissed before the game everyone assumes could deliver the final blow. The decision would have to come during the week after Wisconsin, with Ohio State already waiting on the calendar.

That timing matters. USC can lose badly to Oregon and still tell itself that the next three games will provide more information. It can lose to Washington and still point toward Penn State. It can lose at Penn State and still wait for Wisconsin. When Wisconsin is finished, one enormous game is sitting on the other side of the deadline.

The 28 works against the firing in that narrow sense. A 21-point home loss can keep every part of the Riley conversation alive and still leave the prediction technically wrong. Dan did not pick Oregon to win big. He picked Oregon to win by 28 or more, then asked USC to make a decision before the game most people would expect to settle the matter.

## What I am watching

I am watching the actual margin on September 26 first. Oregon winning by 27 would tell me plenty about both teams, but it would not satisfy this call. I am watching Washington on October 3 and Penn State on October 10 next, because those two games can determine whether the Riley question is still open or has become a decision. I am watching the week after Wisconsin on October 24, because that is when the before-Halloween deadline becomes real.

Ohio State on October 31 is the final piece. If Riley reaches that game, Dan's timing is gone even if the Buckeyes deliver the defeat people expected all along. The death blow arriving on the deadline does not count as before it.

So I am planting this flag without softening it: Oregon will not win at USC by 28 or more, and Lincoln Riley will not be fired before Halloween. I believe the firing is the more attainable half. I do not believe the margin will be there, and the margin is the whole bet.

This call gets graded after the Ohio State game on October 31, with the Oregon margin and Riley's status counted exactly as written. If Dan gets both halves right, the chalice is earned. If Oregon wins by 27, the prediction misses just as surely as it would with a 10-point win.

Vote in the Pulse below and tell me which half you trust: Oregon by 28, or Riley gone before Halloween. The porch can argue about the coach. The scoreboard will settle the number.

— JP

legacyFan.notes: This reads like a machine grinding through a template three times over—by the fourth section restating 'the margin is the bet' I wanted to skip ahead. It's needlessly repetitive (I counted the same point about 27 vs 28 made at least four separate times) and the schedule recap feels like filler pulled from a media guide rather than analysis with stakes. There's no real texture or humor, no line I'd text a friend, just a grading rubric dressed up as a column. Worst offenders: 'That is the tension inside the prediction' and 'The margin supplies the alarm. The schedule supplies the additional evidence'—both sound like a robot summarizing its own argument rather than a guy talking on a porch.

legacyVoice.notes: Draft keeps first-person JP voice and the grading-date device but drops the recurring three-board/two-question structural comparison and the tender warmth toward the reader ('the porch is for'); instead it leans on repetitive short-clause hammering ('Not Oregon. Not even the idea...') and consultant-style breakdowns ('That is the tension inside the prediction,' 'The margin supplies the alarm. The schedule supplies the additional evidence') that read more mechanical than the exemplar's looser, more personal cadence. Sentences like 'The 28 works against the firing in that narrow sense' and 'One is a major loss. The other activates the exact margin that makes this prediction a 9.75' feel like an analyst auditioning conclusions rather than JP's usual conversational verdict-delivery. Paragraph rhythm is closer to the exemplar than most drafts, and the closing direct address to the reader is preserved, keeping this a recognizable but slightly stiffer version of the voice.
